extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of moral philosophy (virtue ethics); instructors and scholars of ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts conceptual criteria for judging actions, moral choice, responsibility, formation of character, and the virtue of courage from a classical virtue-ethics treatment (Aristotle). Useful for evaluating whether actions/habits deserve praise, blame, or moral responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary action (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Voluntary action is 'that whose origination is in the agent, he being aware of the particular details in which the action consists.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voluntary actions originate with the agent and involve awareness of the particulars of the action; children and animals share in voluntary action but not in Moral Choice. Actions done from anger or lust can still be voluntary (they are not automatically involuntary). Examples and discussion show voluntary includes actions one would choose at the time and with the relevant particulars known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compulsory (actions under compulsion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compulsory action is 'that whose origination is from without, the party compelled contributing nothing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compulsion is caused by external forces where the agent contributes nothing. Compulsory actions tend to be accompanied by pain; debate over whether pleasant or honourable things count as compulsion (if so, all actions would be compelled). Example: Alcmaeon's matricide is absurdly excused as compulsion. Actions under compulsion are more like involuntary and lessen praise/blame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Involuntary action (ignorance + remorse)
rubrics_metrics.description: Not every action caused by ignorance is involuntary; 'every action of which ignorance is the cause is not-voluntary, but that only is involuntary which is attended with pain and remorse.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes 'involuntary' (accompanied by pain and regret) from 'not-voluntary' (ignorance without regret). Only when ignorance leads to subsequent sorrow is the act properly called involuntary. This shapes moral responsibility and whether blame is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not-voluntary (ignorance without regret)
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions done by reason of ignorance but not followed by annoyance or regret are 'not-voluntary' rather than involuntary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since the agent feels no remorse, such actions are different from involuntary ones; a proper name distinguishes the moral evaluation. Example: someone who did not know and feels no regret cannot be said to have acted with or against his will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevant particulars for ignorance (when ignorance makes action involuntary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ignorance may be of particulars in which the action consists (who acts, what he is doing, with respect to what or in what, with what instrument, with what result, how).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ignorance about central particulars can render an action involuntary (e.g., Aeschylus unaware of the unlawfulness of speaking of the Mysteries; mistaking a son for an enemy; displaying a catapult without intending harm). Ignorance of general principles is blameworthy; ignorance of specific details relevant to the act can excuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberation (scope and object)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberation 'has for its object whatever may be done through one’s own instrumentality' and is concerned with means to ends, not the ends themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberation applies only to matters under our power and where there is some indefiniteness about how a given end is to be achieved; it excludes eternal, necessary, universally regular, purely chance, or exact/scientific matters. Deliberation is a search into means and practical steps, stopping when a possible course of action is found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral Choice (prohairesis) definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral Choice is 'a grasping after something in our own power consequent upon Deliberation'—voluntary and the result of prior deliberation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral Choice is distinct from wish, desire, opinion, anger, or lust; it concerns means (things in our power) and involves reasoned deliberation. It determines character (choosing good/bad contributes to one's moral makeup) and is the central faculty for moral responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction from Wish, Opinion, Anger, Lust
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral Choice is not identical with Wish (whose object is Ends), Opinion (which can be about eternal or impossible things), Anger, or Lust (which are irrational and shared with animals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wish targets ends and may include impossibles; Opinion divides true/false not good/bad; Anger and Lust can motivate actions but are not the deliberative, voluntary process constitutive of Moral Choice. Moral Choice deals with means under one’s control and is tied to character formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberation excludes trivial sense-details
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberation is not employed on matters of detail that fall under sense (e.g., whether the substance before me is bread or is properly cooked).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one deliberated about every minor perceptual detail one could deliberate ad infinitum. Deliberation concerns practical choices with genuine uncertainty about means, not immediate sensory judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility for habits and character
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtues and vices are formed by repeated actions; the origination of these habits is in our power and therefore voluntary (even if later, being in the habit, one lacks full control).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A person is blameworthy for being vicious if he knowingly did those things by which he became unjust or intemperate; ignorance of the formation of habits is culpable stupidity. Once habits are formed they may limit change, but the original formation is voluntary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Praise and blame depend on voluntariness and preventability
rubrics_metrics.description: People are praised or blamed according as actions are voluntary or not; lawgivers punish those who act wrongly unless compulsion or non-self-caused ignorance excuses them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-caused ignorance (e.g., drunkenness) attracts harsher penalties; those who neglect duties they could have known are blamed. The social practice of reward and punishment presupposes that actions and character are in individuals' power to a significant extent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue as mean state (general criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral Virtues are 'mean states' with respect to two vices (excess and deficiency), formed by habit and to be exercised 'so as right Reason may direct.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Virtue lies between extremes and is determined by the appropriate relation to the object (e.g., fear/confidence for Courage). The mean is relative to us and depends on practical reason; virtues are dispositions to act in the right way, for the right ends, at the right times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage (definition and evaluative criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courage is a mean state 'in respect of fear and boldness' concerning noble/honourable dangers; 'He is Brave who withstands, and fears, and is bold, in respect of right objects, from a right motive, in right manner, and at right times.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courage's proper object is fear of greatest evils (notably death) in the most honourable circumstances (e.g., war). The brave person fears appropriately and acts for honour (the motive) guided by right reason. Wrong objects, wrong manner, wrong time, or wrong motives produce cowardice or rashness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context-sensitivity of fearful objects (for courage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Not every instance of death or danger is the proper object of Courage; context matters (e.g., honourable death in war vs. drowning or sickness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Brave are fearless regarding honourable death and sudden emergencies where one can help oneself; being fearless about non-honourable or unavoidable harms (drowning, sickness) is not the same virtue. Distinguishes kinds of danger and appropriate targets of courageousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excess and deficiency typology (rashness and cowardice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Excess in confidence yields rashness (precipitate, braggart); deficiency yields cowardice (fears wrong objects, at wrong times). The brave person occupies the mean.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rash people are eager before danger but fall away in danger; cowards fear too much and in the wrong way; the brave are composed before danger and quick in action when required. This is the standard evaluative model for virtues generally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different species of 'courage' (degrees and sources)
rubrics_metrics.description: Various dispositions bear the name of Courage by resemblance: civic courage (from shame/honour), compulsion by commanders, skill/experience (soldiers), and mere animal spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True Courage is rooted in sense of honour and aim at the noble. Courage due to compulsion or command, or produced by mere skill or animal impulse, resembles true courage but is inferior: compulsion lacks the honour motive, skill-based bravery collapses when danger exceeds competence, and animal spirit lacks the noble end.
